**Given:** $\overline{BC} \cong \overlin

solution_steps.description:
We have quadrilateral $ABCD$ with diagonal $\overline{AC}$ drawn, splitting it into $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle CDA$.

The key insight: $\overline{AC}$ is **shared** by both triangles, and since $\overline{BC} \parallel \overline{AD}$, the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ acts as a **transversal** — creating a pair of alternate interior angles we can use.

With one shared side, one given pair of congruent sides, and one pair of congruent angles (from parallel lines), we'll have exactly what we need for **SAS** congruence.
solution_steps.title: Understand the Setup

solution_steps.description:
Draw diagonal $\overline{AC}$, which is a side of **both** triangles.

By the **Reflexive Property of Congruence**, any segment is congruent to itself:
$$\overline{AC} \cong \overline{AC}$$

This gives us one pair of congruent sides shared between the two triangles.
solution_steps.title: Mark the Diagonal AC

solution_steps.description:
Since $\overline{BC} \parallel \overline{AD}$, the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ is a transversal cutting those parallel lines.

By the **Alternate Interior Angles Theorem**, the angles on opposite sides of the transversal between the parallel lines are congruent:
$$\angle BCA \cong \angle DAC$$

Notice carefully which angles these are:
- $\angle BCA$ is at vertex $C$, inside $\triangle ABC$, between sides $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AC}$
- $\angle DAC$ is at vertex $A$, inside $\triangle CDA$, between sides $\overline{DA}$ and $\overline{AC}$

The angle sits **between** the two sides we're using — exactly what SAS requires.
solution_steps.title: Identify Alternate Interior Angles

solution_steps.description:
Collect the three facts and match them to the **SAS (Side-Angle-Side)** pattern — two sides and the **included** angle (the angle sandwiched between those two sides):

| $\triangle ABC$ | $\triangle CDA$ | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| $\overline{BC}$ | $\overline{DA}$ | Given |
| $\angle BCA$ | $\angle DAC$ | Alternate Interior Angles |
| $\overline{AC}$ | $\overline{CA}$ | Reflexive Property |

In $\triangle ABC$: the included angle $\angle BCA$ sits between $\overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AC}$. ✓
In $\triangle CDA$: the included angle $\angle DAC$ sits between $\overline{DA}$ and $\overline{CA}$. ✓

All three SAS conditions are met, so:
$$\triangle ABC \cong \triangle CDA \quad \blacksquare$$
solution_steps.title: Apply SAS Congruence

solution_steps.description:
We have two parallel lines, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$, connected by segment $\overline{BC}$, with $M$ the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$.

The key insight: $M$ sits **between** $B$ and $C$, making it the vertex where the two triangles "meet." When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, they produce **alternate interior angles** — and any two lines crossing at a point create **vertical angles**. Those two angle facts, combined with the midpoint, give us exactly three congruent pairs.
solution_steps.title: Understand the Setup

solution_steps.description:
Since $M$ is the **midpoint** of $\overline{BC}$, it divides the segment into two equal halves:
$$BM = MC$$
This is our **congruent side**, and it is the side shared between the two triangles (it lies between the two angles we'll identify next).
solution_steps.title: Pair 1: Midpoint → Equal Sides

solution_steps.description:
Since $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$, and $\overline{BC}$ acts as a **transversal** cutting across those parallel lines, the angles on opposite sides of the transversal between the parallels are **alternate interior angles** — and alternate interior angles are always equal:
$$\angle ABM = \angle DCM$$
Think of it as a "Z" shape formed by the parallel lines and the transversal — the angles inside the Z are equal.
solution_steps.title: Pair 2: Alternate Interior Angles

solution_steps.description:
At point $M$, segments $\overline{AM}$ and $\overline{DM}$ cross. Any two straight lines that cross form **vertical angles** — the angles directly across from each other — and vertical angles are always equal:
$$\angle AMB = \angle DMC$$
This is our second pair of congruent angles, at the other end of side $\overline{BM}$.
solution_steps.title: Pair 3: Vertical Angles

solution_steps.description:
Gathering our three pairs and matching them to $\triangle ABM$ vs. $\triangle DCM$:

| Part | $\triangle ABM$ | $\triangle DCM$ | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| Angle | $\angle ABM$ | $\angle DCM$ | Alternate interior angles, $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$ |
| **Side** | $BM$ | $MC$ | $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ |
| Angle | $\angle AMB$ | $\angle DMC$ | Vertical angles |

The pattern is **Angle–Side–Angle (ASA)**: one angle, the included side between those angles, then the other angle.

The **ASA Congruence Postulate** states: if two angles and the included side of one triangle are congruent to two angles and the included side of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.

Therefore:
$$\triangle ABM \cong \triangle DCM \quad (\text{ASA})$$
